scenes.head: Linking the statements
scenes.sub: Put Lantern’s whole annual report together, check that its four statements articulate and find the error when they don’t, follow single transactions through all of them, see where the gap between profit and cash sits, and push one change through the three main statements the way analysts test a model.

segs.say: Linking the statements. Put Lantern’s whole annual report together, check that its four statements articulate and find the error when they don’t, follow single transactions through all of them, see where the gap between profit and cash sits, and push one change through the three main statements the way analysts test a model.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Trace a transaction through the income statement, the statement of changes in equity, the balance sheet and the statement of cash flows.
Use a preparer’s checklist of links to test whether a set of statements articulates, and locate the error when a link fails.
Locate each part of the gap between Lantern’s net income and its operating cash flow on the balance sheet, and judge which parts will reverse.
Calculate the effect of one change, such as $1,000 more depreciation with tax at 25%, on all three main statements, with the tax paid or still owed.
Interpret the linked statements to judge how much cash a business can afford to distribute.

scenes.head: It is January 2027.

segs.say: It is January 2027. Lantern’s accountant has closed the books for the ten months to 31 December 2026 and drafted the four statements. Before they go to Coastline Bank and to the dealer’s finance company that lent Lantern $20,000 for the van, she checks that they tell one consistent story: every figure that appears in two places must agree, and every change on the balance sheet must be explained somewhere else.

scenes.head: F01 introduced articulation on a single month: net income flows into equity, ending equity into the balance sheet, and ending cash from the statement…

segs.say: F01 introduced articulation on a single month: net income flows into equity, ending equity into the balance sheet, and ending cash from the statement of cash flows into the balance sheet. A full year adds inventory, bad debts, depreciation on two assets, accrued interest, income tax and a second dividend, so there are many more places for a link to break. This lesson puts Lantern’s whole annual report together, shows how a preparer finds an error when a link fails, follows single transactions through all four statements, and walks one change through the three main statements, the way analysts test a financial model.

scenes.head: The idea underneath every link is that comparative balance sheets list balances at two moments, and the other three statements explain how those…

segs.say: The idea underneath every link is that comparative balance sheets list balances at two moments, and the other three statements explain how those balances moved in between. The income statement explains most of the change in retained earnings; the statement of changes in equity explains all of the change in equity; the statement of cash flows explains all of the change in cash. Any other balance sheet change is the other half of an entry whose first half appears on one of those statements, or a noncash investing and financing activity disclosed in a note.
How Lantern’s statements for the ten months to 31 December 2026 articulate (fictional figures in dollars).

scenes.head: Lantern makes the links easy to see because it began on 1 March 2026 with nothing: every opening balance is zero, so every closing balance on its…

segs.say: Lantern makes the links easy to see because it began on 1 March 2026 with nothing: every opening balance is zero, so every closing balance on its balance sheet is also the year’s change. Cash of $42,940 is the year’s increase in cash; retained earnings of $22,387 are the year’s net income less the year’s dividends. From 2027 onward the opening balances will be the 2026 closing balances, and every link will compare two balance sheets.

scenes.head: Three links and one identity

segs.say: Three links and one identity. Net income on the income statement equals net income in the statement of changes in equity. Ending equity there equals equity on the balance sheet. Ending cash on the statement of cash flows equals cash on the balance sheet. And the balance sheet must balance: assets equal liabilities plus equity. A set of statements that passes all four tests is not necessarily right, but one that fails any of them is certainly wrong.

scenes.head: Readers rely on the links as much as preparers do.

segs.say: Readers rely on the links as much as preparers do. A lender who sees profit rising while operating cash flow falls turns to the balance sheet to find where the cash went: into receivables, into inventory, or into paying suppliers faster. An owner who wants to know how much of the profit has been kept in the business looks at retained earnings. Each question is answered by reading two statements together, which only works if they articulate.

scenes.head: Here are the four statements the accountant drafted, in the order F01 taught.

segs.say: Here are the four statements the accountant drafted, in the order F01 taught. The income statement comes first, because net income feeds the statement of changes in equity; that statement comes next, because ending equity feeds the balance sheet; then the balance sheet; then the statement of cash flows, which explains the change in the balance sheet’s cash. The income statement is in the multi-step format and the statement of cash flows uses the direct method, followed by the indirect reconciliation of net income to operating cash flow.
Lantern Coffee Co., Income statement for the ten months ended 31 December 2026
Lantern Coffee Co., Statement of changes in equity for the ten months ended 31 December 2026
Lantern Coffee Co., Balance sheet at 31 December 2026
Lantern Coffee Co., Statement of cash flows (direct method) for the ten months ended 31 December 2026
Lantern Coffee Co., Cash flows from operating activities (indirect method) for the ten months ended 31 December 2026

scenes.head: The notes complete the report: Lantern’s accounting policies (first in, first out for inventory, straight-line depreciation with a full month in the…

segs.say: The notes complete the report: Lantern’s accounting policies (first in, first out for inventory, straight-line depreciation with a full month in the month of purchase, the aging method for bad debts), the terms of its two notes payable, and the noncash part of the van purchase. Under the full disclosure principle a reader shouldn’t have to guess any of them.

scenes.head: Before the statements leave the office, the accountant works through a list of links.

segs.say: Before the statements leave the office, the accountant works through a list of links. Most are tie-outs, a comparison of the same figure in two places; the rest are roll-forwards, which need a short calculation. The last column says what a failed check usually points to, which is where the search for an error starts.
Articulation checks on Lantern’s 2026 statements (fictional figures in dollars)

scenes.head: The last three checks are roll-forwards, which the indirect method lesson used to rebuild cash flows; here they test the statements.

segs.say: The last three checks are roll-forwards, which the indirect method lesson used to rebuild cash flows; here they test the statements. Lantern’s opening balances are zero, but from 2027 every roll-forward starts from the previous year’s closing balance. Accounts receivable rolls forward the same way: opening $0, plus catering invoiced of $59,920, less cash collected of $51,720, less the $820 written off, gives $7,380, the gross balance on the balance sheet.

scenes.head: Passing every check is necessary, not sufficient.

segs.say: Passing every check is necessary, not sufficient. An expense posted to the wrong expense account, a noncurrent asset shown as current, or an adjusting entry left out of the ledger altogether leaves every link intact, because all four statements are drawn from the same ledger. The checks catch omissions and copying errors between the statements; review and judgement catch the rest.

chapters.title: Finding the error when a link fails

scenes.head: When a link fails, the size of the difference is the first clue.

segs.say: When a link fails, the size of the difference is the first clue. A difference equal to one item suggests that item was left out, counted twice, or is a noncash item treated as cash; a difference of exactly twice an item suggests it was entered with the wrong sign. The direction narrows the search further: a statement of cash flows that ends below the balance sheet’s cash has too little coming in or too much going out. Two errors can partly offset, so after fixing the first, measure the difference again; the challenging example below works through such a case.

scenes.head: Following single transactions shows why the links hold.

segs.say: Following single transactions shows why the links hold. Each journal entry changes at least two accounts. When one of them is a revenue, expense or dividends account, the entry reaches equity; when one of them is Cash, it reaches the statement of cash flows. Four of Lantern’s entries show the patterns, and every amount in the income statement column also reaches the statement of changes in equity through net income.
Four Lantern entries traced through the statements (fictional figures in dollars)

scenes.head: The van shows one decision touching every statement at different times.

segs.say: The van shows one decision touching every statement at different times. On 1 June it changed the balance sheet and, for the $10,000 paid, the investing section. The $20,000 borrowed from the dealer’s finance company never passed through Lantern’s bank account, so it is disclosed as a noncash investing and financing activity, and the instalments repaying it from June 2027 will be financing outflows. From June onward the van generated expenses: $400 a month of depreciation and $100 a month of interest (20,000 × 6% ÷ 12), both reducing net income and so retained earnings. At the year end, entry e8 moved the $5,000 due on 1 June 2027 into current liabilities, which changed the balance sheet’s classification and nothing else.

scenes.head: The write-down shows how an entry with no cash still reaches the statement of cash flows.

segs.say: The write-down shows how an entry with no cash still reaches the statement of cash flows. In the indirect method it lowers income before tax by $400 and, after the $100 of tax it saves, net income by $300; it makes the increase in inventory $400 smaller (Lantern’s inventory line, $5,800, is measured after it); and, because Lantern’s 2026 tax is partly unpaid, it makes the increase in income taxes payable $100 smaller. The three effects, −300 + 400 − 100 = 0, cancel, as they must when no cash moves. Bad debt expense works the same way, through the net receivables line ($6,796, which already includes the $1,404 charge) and through income taxes payable.

chapters.title: Where the gap between profit and cash sits

scenes.head: The indirect method lesson reconciled Lantern’s net income of $27,387 with its $39,940 of cash from operations; the question here is where each part…

segs.say: The indirect method lesson reconciled Lantern’s net income of $27,387 with its $39,940 of cash from operations; the question here is where each part of the $12,553 gap sits and what happens to it next. Depreciation of $4,800 is the cost of assets already paid for or financed: the equipment and the van’s $10,000 down payment left through investing, and the $20,000 financed by the van note leaves through financing as it is repaid from June 2027. The $13,536 of operating current assets (net receivables, inventory, supplies and prepaid insurance) sits on the asset side of the balance sheet and turns into cash, or expense, in 2027. The $21,289 of operating current liabilities sits on the other side and financed more than the whole gap, but it reverses early in 2027, when Lantern pays the December bills, the wages and the tax, and delivers $6,100 of service it has already been paid for. A first year flatters operating cash flow this way, because a new business has no old liabilities to pay off, so a lender who projected $39,940 a year forward would be overestimating.

scenes.head: Analysts test their understanding of the links, and their spreadsheet models, by pushing one change through all three main statements.

segs.say: Analysts test their understanding of the links, and their spreadsheet models, by pushing one change through all three main statements. The standard exercise: suppose depreciation is $1,000 higher, tax is 25% of income before tax, and the change in tax is paid in cash within the year.
Income statement. Operating income and income before tax fall by $1,000. Income tax falls by 25% × 1,000 = 250, so net income falls by 1,000 − 250 = 750.

Statement of cash flows. Net income is $750 lower, but the $1,000 of depreciation is added back, so operating cash flow rises by −750 + 1,000 = 250: the tax saved. Investing and financing are unchanged.

Balance sheet. Cash is $250 higher. Accumulated depreciation is $1,000 higher, so property and equipment (net) is $1,000 lower, and total assets fall by $750. Retained earnings fall by the $750 drop in net income. Assets −750 = liabilities 0 + equity −750: the balance sheet still balances.

scenes.head: Lantern’s own books add a twist.

segs.say: Lantern’s own books add a twist. Its estimated tax payments were fixed at $6,000, and entry e9 sets Income Taxes Payable at the year’s tax expense less that amount, so none of a change in its 2026 tax is paid within 2026. If depreciation were $1,000 higher, the tax expense would be $250 lower and so would the payable; the saving would reach cash only when the 2026 tax is paid in 2027. For 2026, then: net income −750, depreciation +1,000, change in income taxes payable −250, so operating cash flow is unchanged; on the balance sheet, assets −1,000 = liabilities −250 + equity −750.

scenes.head: Book tax and real tax

segs.say: Book tax and real tax. Like the case, this lesson assumes income tax is 25% of income before tax. Real tax returns follow their own depreciation rules, so the tax a business pays for a year is not exactly 25% of its accounting profit; accountants record the difference as deferred tax, a topic for intermediate accounting.

scenes.head: Reading the size of a failed cash link

segs.say: Reading the size of a failed cash link: Gap = begincases X item omitted, counted twice, or noncash treated as cash; 2X item entered with the wrong sign endcases.
Gap: Ending cash on the draft statement of cash flows minus cash on the balance sheet (or the reverse) ($).
X: The amount of the item that is wrong ($).
It assumes this: One error at a time. Two errors can partly offset, so measure the gap again after correcting the first.
Hatherley Print Studio: after the unpaid dividend is removed, a gap of 6,400 = 2 × 3,200 points to the sign of the $3,200 change in receivables.

scenes.head: After-tax effect of a change in a pretax expense

segs.say: After-tax effect of a change in a pretax expense: Δ NI = −(1 − t) Δ X.
Δ NI: Change in net income ($).
Δ X: Change in an expense deducted before tax (positive when the expense rises) ($).
t: Tax rate on income before tax, as a decimal.
It assumes this: Tax is a fixed share of income before tax, as in the Lantern case (25%).

scenes.head: Cash and tax payable after a change in a noncash expense

segs.say: Cash and tax payable after a change in a noncash expense: Δ CFO = t × p × Δ N, Δ Tax payable = −t × (1 − p) × Δ N.
Δ CFO: Change in cash from operating activities ($).
Δ Tax payable: Change in income taxes payable at the year end ($).
Δ N: Change in a tax-deductible noncash expense, such as depreciation or a write-down ($).
t: Tax rate on income before tax, as a decimal.
p: Share of the change in tax that is paid within the year (1 if all of it, 0 if none).
It assumes this: The expense itself moves no cash; only the tax it changes does, and only when that tax is paid.
$1,000 more depreciation at 25%: with p = 1, Δ CFO = 250; for Lantern in 2026, p = 0, so Δ CFO = 0 and income taxes payable fall by 250.

chapters.title: Example: Finding the missing links for a bakery

scenes.head: Finding the missing links for a bakery

segs.say: Thornwick Bakery Inc., a fictional company, has drafted its statements for the year. Retained earnings were $30,000 at the start of the year and $66,000 at the end; net income was $48,000. Cash was $9,000 at the start of the year; operating activities provided $52,000, investing activities used $35,000 and financing activities used $10,000. The balance sheet shows cash of $16,000, total assets of $214,000, liabilities of $98,000 and common stock of $50,000. The dividends figure is missing from the draft: find it, and check the links.

scenes.head: Finding the missing links for a bakery

segs.say: Step 1. Retained earnings link, solved for dividends: D = RE_(beg) + NI − RE_(end) = 30,000 + 48,000 − 66,000 = 12,000.
Step 2. Cash link: 9,000 + 52,000 − 35,000 − 10,000 = 16,000, the balance sheet’s cash. The statement of cash flows explains the whole change in cash, 16,000 − 9,000 = 7,000.
Step 3. Equity link: total equity = 50,000 + 66,000 = 116,000, assuming no stock was issued during the year.
Step 4. Balance sheet: 98,000 + 116,000 = 214,000, equal to total assets.

scenes.head: Finding the missing links for a bakery

segs.say: Dividends were $12,000. Every link holds: retained earnings 30,000 + 48,000 − 12,000 = 66,000; cash 9,000 + 52,000 − 35,000 − 10,000 = 16,000; assets $214,000 = liabilities $98,000 + equity $116,000.

The links let a reader recover a figure that isn’t printed: dividends declared follow from the opening and closing retained earnings and net income. Thornwick paid out a quarter of its profit (12,000 ÷ 48,000) and kept the rest in the business. Passing every check shows the statements are consistent, not that every figure in them is right.

chapters.title: Example: A statement of cash flows that doesn’t tie

scenes.head: A statement of cash flows that doesn’t tie

segs.say: Hatherley Print Studio Inc., a fictional company, began the year with cash of $14,300 and retained earnings of $22,000. Its draft statement of cash flows, prepared by the indirect method, is below; it ends at $19,800, but the balance sheet, taken from the ledger, shows cash of $22,400. The balance sheet also shows retained earnings of $54,200 and a $9,000 dividend payable: the board declared a dividend on 15 December, payable on 10 January. Net income was $41,200. Find the errors and correct the statement.

scenes.head: A statement of cash flows that doesn’t tie

segs.say: Step 1. Retained earnings link: 22,000 + 41,200 − 9,000 = 54,200, which agrees with the balance sheet. A dividend reduces retained earnings when it is declared, paid or not, so this link can’t reveal whether the dividend was paid.
Step 2. Cash link: the draft ends at 19,800 but the balance sheet shows 22,400, so the draft is 22,400 − 19,800 = 2,600 short.

Step 3. The dividend payable says the $9,000 was not paid in the year, yet the draft shows it as paid. Removing it raises financing to −8,000 and the ending cash to 19,800 + 9,000 = 28,800, now 28,800 − 22,400 = 6,400 too high.

Step 4. A remaining difference of exactly twice an item points to a sign error: 6,400 = 2 × 3,200. Receivables increased, which ties up cash, so the change must be subtracted. Operating cash flow becomes 41,200 + 6,500 − 3,200 − 2,700 + 1,800 = 43,600.

Step 5. Corrected ending cash: 14,300 + 43,600 − 27,500 − 8,000 = 22,400, the balance sheet’s figure. The unpaid dividend appears as a current liability, not as a cash flow; it will be a financing outflow next year, when it is paid.

scenes.head: A statement of cash flows that doesn’t tie

segs.say: Two errors: the unpaid $9,000 dividend shown as paid, and the $3,200 increase in receivables added instead of subtracted. Corrected: operating activities $43,600; investing ($27,500); financing ($8,000); ending cash $22,400, as on the balance sheet.

The two errors partly offset, so the $2,600 difference matched neither of them. Working through the links one at a time, and using the clue that a difference of exactly twice an item points to a sign error, found both. The corrected statement also changes the story: operations provided $6,400 less cash than the draft claimed.

chapters.title: Example: How much cash can Ana take out of Lantern?

scenes.head: How much cash can Ana take out of Lantern?

segs.say: In January 2027 Ana asks whether Lantern can pay her a $20,000 dividend. Use the 2026 statements: retained earnings $22,387; cash $42,940; current liabilities $26,289, of which $6,100 is unearned revenue. Lantern’s fixed cash costs in 2027 are kitchen rent of $1,200 a month, shop and office wages at 2026’s rate ($18,400 for the ten months) and the $48,000 a year salary Lantern pays Ana from 2027. Assume Lantern wants to keep at least three months of those fixed costs in the bank as a cushion.

scenes.head: How much cash can Ana take out of Lantern?

segs.say: Step 1. Earnings test: a $20,000 dividend is within retained earnings of $22,387, so it would not pay out more profit than Lantern has kept.

Step 2. Cash already claimed: current liabilities of 26,289 include 6,100 of unearned revenue, which Lantern settles by delivering service, not by paying cash. The rest, 26,289 − 6,100 = 20,189, needs cash within the year, including the $5,000 van instalment and $3,129 of tax.
Step 3. Cash left after those payments: 42,940 − 20,189 = 22,751.

Step 4. Cushion: monthly fixed cash costs in 2027 are rent 1,200 + shop and office wages 18,400 ÷ 10 = 1,840 + Ana’s salary 48,000 ÷ 12 = 4,000, so 7,040. Three months is 3 × 7,040 = 21,120, and the largest dividend that keeps the cushion is about 22,751 − 21,120 = 1,631.

Step 5. Timing: $21,289 of 2026’s operating cash flow came from operating liabilities that reverse in 2027; delivering the $6,100 of prepaid service will use cash (baristas, beans, materials) without bringing any in; and the insurance policy expires on 28 February 2027 and must be renewed. The cushion is not generous.

scenes.head: How much cash can Ana take out of Lantern?

segs.say: A $20,000 dividend passes the earnings test but fails the cash test: it would leave about $2,751 after known payments, less than half a month of 2027’s fixed costs. On these assumptions a dividend of about $1,600 is the most Lantern can afford now; a larger one should wait until 2027’s own operating cash has come in, and Ana should check the loan agreements first, since lenders’ covenants often limit dividends.

Retained earnings show how much of the profit earned has been kept in the business; state law and lenders’ covenants set what Lantern may legally distribute, and the balance sheet and the statement of cash flows show what it can afford. Here the linked statements also explain why the bank balance looks bigger than the business’s spare cash: much of it is owed to suppliers, staff, lenders and the tax authorities, or has been paid by customers for work still to do.

scenes.head: An interactive

segs.say: Analyse seven of Lantern’s entries, from the van in June to the year-end income tax. For each, choose the accounts, the sides and the amounts, then tick every statement it changes and, if cash moves, the activity. Watch for the entries that change the statement of cash flows without touching the income statement, and the reverse. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “Tax can be left out of a three-statement walkthrough.”

segs.say: “Tax can be left out of a three-statement walkthrough.”. Without tax, $1,000 more depreciation would lower net income by $1,000 and leave cash unchanged. With tax at 25%, net income falls by only $750, and the $250 of tax saved is cash once the tax is paid. Every pretax change has a tax echo on all three statements: in income tax expense, in cash or income taxes payable, and in retained earnings.

scenes.head: “If the balance sheet balances, the statements are right.”

segs.say: “If the balance sheet balances, the statements are right.”. Balancing is one test among several. Hatherley Print Studio’s balance sheet balanced while its statement of cash flows was wrong in two places. Run every link, and remember that some errors, such as an expense posted to the wrong expense account, break none of them.

scenes.head: “A dividend reduces cash when it is declared.”

segs.say: “A dividend reduces cash when it is declared.”. Declaring a dividend reduces retained earnings and creates Dividends Payable; cash falls only when it is paid, and that payment is the financing outflow. A December declaration paid in January appears in this year’s statement of changes in equity and next year’s statement of cash flows.

scenes.head: “The tax saved by an extra expense is always cash this year.”

segs.say: “The tax saved by an extra expense is always cash this year.”. Only if the change in tax is paid within the year. Lantern’s estimated payments were fixed at $6,000, so $1,000 more depreciation would lower income taxes payable by $250 and leave 2026’s operating cash flow unchanged; the cash saving arrives when the tax is paid in 2027.

scenes.head: “Operating cash flow above net income is always good news.”

segs.say: “Operating cash flow above net income is always good news.”. Lantern’s operating cash flow exceeds its net income by $12,553, but $21,289 of its operating cash came from liabilities that will be paid, or worked off, early in 2027. Read where each part of the gap sits before drawing a conclusion from its size.

scenes.head: “An entry with no cash never appears in the statement of cash flows.”

segs.say: “An entry with no cash never appears in the statement of cash flows.”. It never changes a cash total, but it can still appear. The accrued interest (e5) shows up in Lantern’s indirect reconciliation as an increase in interest payable, offsetting its effect on net income and on income taxes payable, and the $20,000 van note appears in the noncash disclosure beneath the statement. Count an entry as a cash flow only when cash moves.

scenes.head: Coastline Bank’s credit analyst receives Lantern’s annual report in February 2027.

segs.say: Coastline Bank’s credit analyst receives Lantern’s annual report in February 2027. Before calculating anything she repeats the accountant’s checks, because statements that don’t articulate can’t be relied on, and then reads the statements in pairs. The income statement and the statement of cash flows together show that Lantern’s operations produced more cash than profit; the balance sheet shows why: $21,289 of operating liabilities, most of which fall due early in 2027.

scenes.head: Her next step is a forecast for 2027, which she builds as a three-statement model.

segs.say: Her next step is a forecast for 2027, which she builds as a three-statement model. Assumptions about sales, margins, how quickly customers pay and suppliers are paid, and capital spending drive a forecast income statement and balance sheet; the statement of cash flows is derived from the changes between the two balance sheets. The links are the model’s skeleton. Forecast net income feeds retained earnings, forecast depreciation feeds accumulated depreciation and the add-back, and the van note’s $5,000 instalment reduces both cash and the liability. If the forecast balance sheet doesn’t balance, a link is missing, and she finds it the way the accountant finds errors in a draft: by the size and direction of the difference.

scenes.head: The model answers the lender’s real question: can Lantern pay the $5,000 instalment and $1,200 of interest due on the van note on 1 June 2027, and…

segs.say: The model answers the lender’s real question: can Lantern pay the $5,000 instalment and $1,200 of interest due on the van note on 1 June 2027, and $600 of interest on the Coastline note during the year, from its own operations, now that it also pays Ana a salary? Read together, the 2026 statements suggest it can, provided the first year’s timing benefit is not mistaken for a permanent level of cash flow. Ratios that summarise this kind of judgement, such as cash flow relative to debt payments, belong to F03; the reasoning they rest on is the articulation in this lesson.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Comparative balance sheets list balances at two moments; the income statement, the statement of changes in equity and the statement of cash flows explain how they moved in between.

Three links and one identity: net income to the statement of changes in equity, ending equity to the balance sheet, ending cash to the balance sheet, and assets = liabilities + equity. Lantern: 27,387; 42,387; 42,940; 93,676 = 51,289 + 42,387.

Roll-forwards (opening + movements = closing) extend the checks to tax, interest, accumulated depreciation and receivables. When a link fails, a gap equal to an item suggests an omission and twice an item a sign error.

A transaction reaches equity through any revenue, expense or dividend it touches and the statement of cash flows through any cash it moves; an entry with no cash changes no cash total, though it may appear as offsetting reconciliation lines or in the noncash disclosure.

Lantern’s $12,553 gap between operating cash flow and net income sits in three places: depreciation of $4,800 on assets already paid for or financed, $13,536 of operating current assets, and $21,289 of operating current liabilities that reverse early in 2027.

One change through three statements: $1,000 more depreciation at 25% lowers net income by $750; operating cash flow rises by $250 only if the change in tax is paid within the year, otherwise income taxes payable fall instead.

Retained earnings show how much of the profit earned has been kept in the business; state law and lenders’ covenants set what it may legally distribute, and the balance sheet and the statement of cash flows show what it can afford.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
